questions.question: A continuous life annuity pays at rate one per year while its recipient is alive. Ignoring interest, what amount does it pay during a surviving interval of length $h>0$ years?

A continuous life annuity pays at rate one while alive, with present value $Y=\int_0^T \mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\,\mathrm{d}t$ for future lifetime $T$ and constant interest force $\delta>0$. In the limiting case $T=0$, does it make a certain unit payment at issue?
options: No; its present value is zero.
Yes; its present value is one.

questions.question: A rate-one continuous life annuity has realised future lifetime $T\ge0$ and discount force $\delta=0$. Which formula gives its present value $Y$ for every such lifetime?

A continuous annuity pays at rate one until random future lifetime $T$ ends. Interest force $\delta$ is fixed and $S(t)=\mathbb{P}(T>t)$. Which quantity varies between lives with different realised lifetimes under this same model?

A rate-one continuous life annuity has survivor $S(t)$, mortality force $\mu(t)$ and interest force $\delta$. Why does its APV integrand use $\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}S(t)$ rather than $\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\mu(t)$?
options: The mortality force is a survival probability with the discount already included.
A death rate determines the number of live annuity payments directly.
Payment at time t requires being alive, not a death rate at that time.
Survival weighting is needed only when interest is zero.

questions.question: A rate-one continuous annuity stops at the realised death time $T=2$ years. Its interest force is $\delta=\log 2$ per year. What is its realised present value $Y$?
A continuous annuity pays at rate $100$ per year. The lifetime has constant mortality force $\lambda=0.02$ per year, and interest force is $\delta=0.03$ per year. What is its actuarial present value?

A rate-one continuous annuity has positive interest force $\delta=0.05$ per year and a finite realised lifetime $T$. Which relation holds between its present value $Y=\int_0^T \mathrm{e}^{-0.05t}\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $20$?
options: $0\le Y\le20$, and $Y=20$ at some finite lifetime.

questions.question: For the same lifetime $T$, define unit death-discount APV $D=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-\delta T}]$ and rate-one continuous annuity APV $a=\mathbb{E}[\int_0^T \mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\,\mathrm{d}t]$. With $\delta=0.03$ per year and $D=0.4$, what is $a$?
A rate-one continuous life annuity has APV $a=5$ under a fixed lifetime and interest model. An otherwise identical annuity pays at rate $3$ per year. What is its APV?

For interest force $\delta>0$, let $F(t)=\int_0^t \mathrm{e}^{-\delta s}\,\mathrm{d}s$ be the present value of a rate-one continuous annuity lasting exactly $t$ years. How does extending its lifetime affect the accumulated value and the marginal accrual rate?
options: Value decreases, while the marginal accrual rate increases.
Value increases at a constant marginal accrual rate of one.
Value is unchanged once the first year has been completed.
Value increases, while the marginal accrual rate decreases.

questions.question: Two rate-one continuous annuities use the same interest force $\delta\ge0$. Their survivor functions satisfy $S_1(t)\ge S_2(t)$ for every $t\ge0$, and both APVs $a_1,a_2$ are finite. What comparison is guaranteed?

A rate-one continuous annuity has APV $12$ under constant mortality force $\lambda>0$ and constant interest force $\delta\ge0$, both unknown. What combination of these two rates does this single quote identify?

A rate-one continuous annuity has lifetime survivor $S(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-(\log3)t}$ and interest force $\delta=\log2$. Its realised value is $Y=(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\delta T})/\delta$, where $T$ is future lifetime. What is $\mathbb{P}(Y>1/(2\log2))$?

A continuous annuity pays at rate one until death or time $n=2$ years, whichever comes first. Mortality force is $\lambda=\log2$ per year and interest force is $\delta=\log2$ per year. What is its APV?
At zero interest, a rate-one continuous annuity has survivor $S(t)=1-t/4$ for $0\le t\le4$ and zero thereafter. What is its APV?

A future lifetime has survivor $S(t)=1/(1+t)$ for $t\ge0$. A rate-one continuous annuity uses interest force $\delta=1$ per year and APV $a$. What can be concluded about finiteness of $a$ and of the mean lifetime $\mathbb{E}[T]$?
options: The annuity APV is finite, but the mean lifetime is infinite.
Both the annuity APV and the mean lifetime are finite.
Both the annuity APV and the mean lifetime are infinite.
The annuity APV and mean lifetime are equal finite numbers.

questions.question: At interest force $\delta=1$, two rate-one continuous annuities have lifetimes uniform on $(0,2)$ and $(0.5,1.5)$ respectively; both means are one year. Their APVs are $a_A=(1+\mathrm{e}^{-2})/2$ and $a_B=1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}+\mathrm{e}^{-1.5}$. What does their comparison show?
options: Equal mean lifetimes guarantee equal APVs for any fixed interest force.
The second APV is smaller because its minimum lifetime is larger.
Equal mean lifetimes need not give equal discounted annuity APVs.
A uniform lifetime makes each APV equal to its mean lifetime at positive interest.

questions.question: Under unknown constant mortality force $\lambda>0$ and interest force $\delta>0$, a rate-one continuous annuity has APV $a=10$ and unit death-discount APV $D=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-\delta T}]=0.2$. Which pair of rates fits both quotes?

Two zero-interest rate-one continuous annuities share first-year mortality force $\log2$. Thereafter Model A keeps that force, while Model B doubles it. Their one-year survival is $1/2$. What are their whole-life APVs $(a_A,a_B)$?
